aura: The discount isn't the store being generous; it's the brand and the bank paying to get in front of you. The real money is in the warranty and the cable you add at the counter.
facts: Extended warranties often earn a retailer far more than the product they cover.
Many 'discounts' are partly paid by the brand or your bank, not the store.
A retailer can profit from selling goods before it has paid the supplier for them.
Croma is run by Infiniti Retail, a Tata Group company.
hook: When a TV is 'Rs 8,000 off' on Croma's shelf, the store may be earning more on it than on the full-price one. The discount is often a bill paid by someone else.
question: next article on croma / vijay sales model, how they work and earn money by giving so much discount

sections.body:
Electronics retail is a low-margin business. On a phone or laptop, a retailer typically keeps a single-digit percentage of the price. On a Rs 70,000 phone, that might be only a few thousand rupees before rent, staff and electricity are paid.

So the model is volume plus speed. Stock that sells fast and gets paid for quickly can earn more over a year than a high-margin item that sits on the shelf. Think of it like IndiGo: tiny profit per seat, but the plane must always be full.

Croma (a Tata Group company, run by Infiniti Retail) and Vijay Sales (a family-run chain, strong in Mumbai and western India) both play this game, with hundreds of stores between them.

Much of that 'Rs 8,000 off' does not come out of the retailer's pocket.

**Brand-funded discounts:** Samsung, LG, Sony and others often give retailers support money to hit a sales target or clear last year's model. The brand wants market share; the store is the delivery channel.

**Bank offers:** The '10% instant cashback on HDFC cards' is typically funded by the bank (and sometimes shared with the brand), because the bank wants you swiping its card. The same logic sits behind the 'No-cost EMI' we covered earlier.

**Volume rebates:** Retailers reportedly earn back-end incentives from brands. Cross a quarterly sales target, and you get a bonus on every unit sold, sometimes even the ones already sold at a thin margin.

So the sticker shows a big discount, but three different parties may be chipping in.
sections.h: Who really pays for the discount

sections.body:
Imagine a 55-inch TV with a Rs 60,000 MRP, sold at Rs 42,000. The numbers below are illustrative, not actual company figures.

The store buys it from the brand for about Rs 37,000. Brand support of Rs 2,000 and a bank cashback of Rs 2,000 are paid by others. The store's price cut is Rs 18,000 from MRP, but its own cost is far smaller. It collects Rs 42,000 from you and effectively gets some of the rest from the brand and bank.

Add a Rs 3,000 extended warranty, which typically carries a very high margin, and a Rs 1,500 HDMI cable and wall mount. The TV itself might earn Rs 3,000 to 5,000, while the add-ons can earn nearly as much. That is why staff ask, 'Do you want the extended warranty?'

**Float:** Retailers often negotiate credit from suppliers, so they sell the product before they pay for it. That gap is free working capital.

**Add-ons:** Warranties, installation, accessories and protection plans have much higher margins than the devices.

**Own brands and financing tie-ups:** Stores may earn commissions when a lender finances your purchase.

**Footfall:** A cheap deal on a headline product brings you in. You may leave with a soundbar too.

**Online rivalry:** Amazon and Flipkart pushed prices down, so physical chains matched prices and sold the experience instead: touch, demo, same-day installation, and a store to visit when something breaks.

Big-ticket electronics are things people want to see first. A fridge or AC also needs delivery and installation, and a brand-authorised store gives a feeling of safety.

The chains also use that trust to push higher-margin upgrades: a bigger TV, a better model, a bundle. You came for the discount, but the real profit is in the basket you build around it.

title: How Croma and Vijay Sales profit while discounting
